name: AI-Powered Differentiation
objectives: Given one task you teach, explain differentiation by readiness, interest and learning preference, and describe what AI does and what the teacher decides, keeping the same learning goal in every version
Given one learning objective and an AI assistant, create a five-question pre-assessment with a key and three tiered tasks, with all three tiers practicing the same objective
Given one skill to practice, create a nine-square choice board with a must-do square, with every square practicing the skill and taking about the same time
Given pre-assessment results for a made-up class, group students from evidence and write when and how they move between groups, using codes instead of names and no fixed groups
When planning a differentiated lesson, plan the routines, task cards and timing for the class, covering how students find their task, what to do when stuck and what to do when finished
Given a finished differentiated lesson, check it for same goal, movement, patterns and access, and fix anything that fails, passing all four fairness checks

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Differentiation in one minute, and where AI helps
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain differentiation by readiness, interest and learning preference, and name AI's role.
This lesson builds toward: Given one task you teach, you will explain differentiation by readiness, interest and learning preference, and describe what AI does and what the teacher decides, keeping the same learning goal in every version.
Differentiation means adjusting how students reach the same learning goal. Teachers commonly differentiate by readiness (what a student already knows and can do), interest (what engages them) and learning preference (for example, reading, discussing, drawing or building). The goal stays the same; the path changes.
AI helps with the slow part: producing several versions of a task, a set of interest-based examples, or a range of practice. It can turn one problem set into three, or one reading into versions about sports, music and cooking with the same skill.
AI does not know your students. The teacher decides the goal, reads the evidence, chooses who gets which path, and checks every version for accuracy and fairness.
Words to know:
- Differentiation: adjusting how students reach the same learning goal.
- Readiness: what a student already knows and can do on a skill.
- Learning preference: a way a student often learns well, such as discussing or drawing.
Try it now: Take one task you teach. Ask AI to rewrite it three ways for different interests (for example sports, music, cooking) with the same skill. Check each keeps the skill.
You can now explain differentiation and use AI to produce versions of a task while you make the decisions.

check.q: What changes when you differentiate a lesson?
options: The path students take to the goal
The learning goal itself
The grade-level standard
Which students take the final test
check.why: In differentiation the goal stays the same; only the path changes.

check.q: AI turns your reading task into a sports version, a music version and a cooking version. What would you do next?
options: Hand them out without reading them
Check that each version still practices the same skill
Give the sports version to every student
Ask AI to choose which student gets each version
check.why: AI makes the versions, but the teacher checks them and decides who gets which one.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Pre-assessments and tiered tasks
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a quick pre-assessment and three tiered tasks toward one objective.
This lesson builds toward: Given one learning objective and an AI assistant, you will create a five-question pre-assessment with a key and three tiered tasks, with all three tiers practicing the same objective.
Start with evidence. Ask AI for a five-question pre-assessment on the objective: two questions on the prerequisite skills, two on the objective itself, one stretch question. Ask for a key and what each wrong answer suggests. Check every item.
Tiered tasks reach the same objective at different levels of support and complexity. Prompt: "Objective: [paste]. Write three tasks. Tier 1: more support (worked example, steps, word bank). Tier 2: on level. Tier 3: extension (a harder or real-world transfer task). All three must practice the objective. Include answer keys."
Check that Tier 1 is not just easier, but supported toward the same goal, and that Tier 3 is deeper, not just more work. Students in every tier should finish having practiced the objective.
Step by step:
- Ask for a five-question pre-assessment with a key.
- Check every item and the key.
- Ask for three tiers toward the same objective.
- Tier 1 supported, not easier; Tier 3 deeper, not longer.
- Check all keys.
Words to know:
- Pre-assessment: a short check before teaching to see what students already know.
- Tiered task: versions of a task at different levels of support or complexity, aimed at the same goal.
- Transfer task: using a skill in a new, often real-world, situation.
Try it now: Write a five-question pre-assessment and three tiered tasks for one objective with AI. Check that all three tiers practice the same objective.
You can now create a pre-assessment and tiered tasks that all reach the same goal.

check.q: What should a five-question pre-assessment from this lesson include?
options: Five stretch questions
Five questions on last year's unit
Two prerequisite questions, two on the objective and one stretch question
Only questions students will surely get right
check.why: The mix shows who needs prerequisite help, who is ready and who is ready for more.

check.q: Your Tier 3 task is the Tier 2 task with twice as many problems. What would you do?
options: Keep it, because more work is harder
Remove Tier 3
Give it to the support group
Replace it with a deeper task, such as using the skill in a new situation
check.why: Tier 3 should be deeper, not just more work.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Choice boards
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a nine-square choice board for practice with AI.
This lesson builds toward: Given one skill to practice, you will create a nine-square choice board with a must-do square, with every square practicing the skill and taking about the same time.
A choice board is a grid of activities, often nine squares, that all practice the same skill in different ways: write, draw, explain aloud, solve, build, teach someone. Students choose a set number, for example three in a row.
Prompt: "Make a 3 by 3 choice board for 6th graders practicing [skill]. Each square is a different way to practice: writing, drawing, discussing, solving problems, creating, real-world. Every square must practice the skill. Put a must-do square in the middle."
Check that every square truly practices the skill and takes about the same time, and that materials are available. Choice increases engagement; it should never become a way to avoid the hard part.
Step by step:
- Name the skill and grade.
- Ask for a 3 by 3 board with varied ways to practice.
- Make the center square a must-do.
- Check every square practices the skill and is about equal in time.
- Check materials are available.
Words to know:
- Choice board: a grid of activities that practice the same skill in different ways, from which students choose.
- Must-do: an activity every student completes.
Try it now: Build a 3 by 3 choice board with AI for one skill. Check each square and replace any that do not practice the skill.
You can now create choice boards that offer real choice while practicing the same skill.

options: A grid of activities that all practice the same skill in different ways
A list of different topics students can skip
A seating chart
A board where students vote on homework
check.why: Every square practices the same skill; only the way of practicing changes.

check.q: One square on your AI-made choice board asks students to draw their favorite animal, which does not practice the skill. What would you do?
options: Keep it so students have a fun choice
Make it the must-do square
Replace it with a square that practices the skill
Remove the whole board
check.why: Choice should never become a way to avoid the skill.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Flexible grouping from evidence
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Group students from pre-assessment evidence and plan how they move.
This lesson builds toward: Given pre-assessment results for a made-up class, you will group students from evidence and write when and how they move between groups, using codes instead of names and no fixed groups.
Flexible groups change often, based on current evidence for a specific skill, not on a label. After the pre-assessment, sort results into groups for this objective: needs prerequisite support, ready for the objective, ready for extension.
AI can help you see patterns, but student scores with names are education records. Either do the sorting yourself in your gradebook, use a district-approved tool, or replace names with codes before using AI. Practice with a made-up class.
Plan movement: after each check (an exit ticket, a hinge question), students move to the group that fits now. Write when you will re-check and how a student moves up. Groups that never change become tracking.
Step by step:
- Sort pre-assessment results by skill, not label.
- Use your gradebook or an approved tool; never names in unapproved tools.
- Form three groups for this objective.
- Plan re-checks after each lesson.
- Move students as evidence changes.
Words to know:
- Flexible grouping: grouping students by current evidence on a skill, changing often.
- Tracking: keeping students in the same level group for a long time, which can limit opportunity.
Official sources:
- FERPA: Protecting Student Privacy
Try it now: Make up pre-assessment results for 24 students using codes (S1 to S24). Form three groups for the objective and write when and how students will move between them.
You can now group students flexibly from evidence and keep groups moving.

options: Students choose any group they like
It changes often, based on current evidence for a skill
It stays the same all year
It is based on a student's label
check.why: Flexible groups follow current evidence and change as students learn.

check.q: You want AI to help you see patterns in your class's pre-assessment scores. What would you do first?
options: Paste the gradebook with names
Email the scores to a colleague
Post the scores on the wall
Replace names with codes like S1, or use a district-approved tool
check.why: Student scores with names are education records, so protect them before using AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Running a differentiated class
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan the routines that make a differentiated lesson work in the room.
This lesson builds toward: When planning a differentiated lesson, you will plan the routines, task cards and timing for the class, covering how students find their task, what to do when stuck and what to do when finished.
Differentiated lessons fail on logistics more than on materials. Plan routines: how students know their task (a slide or card with group names or colors), where materials are, what to do when stuck ("ask three before me", a help card), and what to do when finished (the choice board).
Plan your time: start with a short whole-class mini-lesson, then meet with the group that needs you most while others work, then check in with each group. AI can draft task cards, help cards and a timing plan.
Make it feel normal. Use neutral group names (colors or shapes, not "low" and "high"), change groups often, and let every group do interesting work. Students notice when one group always gets the dull tasks.
Step by step:
- Show each group its task clearly.
- Set materials, stuck and finished routines.
- Mini-lesson, then teacher time with the neediest group.
- Check in with every group.
- Use neutral names and interesting work for all.
Words to know:
- Routine: a regular way of doing something that students learn and follow.
- Small-group instruction: the teacher teaching a few students at once while others work.
Try it now: Use AI to draft task cards for your three tiers, a help card for when students are stuck, and a timing plan for a 50-minute class.
You can now run a differentiated lesson with clear routines and fair group practices.

check.q: Why do differentiated lessons most often fail?
options: Logistics and routines
Too few worksheets
Students dislike choice
AI makes too many versions
check.why: The lesson says they fail on logistics more than on materials.

check.q: Students finish their tier task ten minutes early. What should your plan tell them to do?
options: Wait quietly
Start the next tier's task
Go to the choice board
Join the teacher's group
check.why: The plan should say what to do when finished, such as the choice board.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Checking differentiation for fairness
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check that differentiation opens doors rather than lowering expectations.
This lesson builds toward: Given a finished differentiated lesson, you will check it for same goal, movement, patterns and access, and fix anything that fails, passing all four fairness checks.
Differentiation can quietly become lower expectations: some students always get easier tasks and never reach the grade-level goal. Check four things. Same goal: does every student practice the grade-level objective? Movement: did students change groups over the unit?
Patterns: look (with privacy protections) at who ends up in each group over time. If students from one background, English learners or students with disabilities are always in the support group, ask why. Access: do supports such as read-aloud or visuals reach every student who needs them, including required IEP and 504 accommodations?
AI materials need the same check: are examples and names varied and respectful, free of stereotypes about who is good at what? Leaders can ask teams to bring one differentiated lesson to a meeting and run this check together.
Step by step:
- Same goal for every tier?
- Did students move between groups?
- Who is always in which group, and why?
- Do supports and required accommodations reach everyone?
- Are AI examples varied and free of stereotypes?
Words to know:
- Expectations: what teachers believe students can achieve, which shapes what they are taught.
- Stereotype: an unfair, fixed idea about a group of people.
Try it now: Final task: assemble your differentiated lesson (pre-assessment with key, three tiers, choice board, grouping plan from made-up data with movement rules), then run the four fairness checks on it and fix anything that fails.
You can now differentiate lessons with AI in a way that keeps expectations high for every student.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Pre-assessment Fewer than five questions, no key, or no link to the objective. Five questions (prerequisites, objective, stretch) with a key. The key also says what each wrong answer suggests. Tiered tasks The tiers practice different goals, or Tier 3 is just more work. Three tiers (more support, on level, extension) all practice the same objective, with keys. Tier 1 has clear supports and Tier 3 is a real transfer task. Choice board Some squares do not practice the skill. Nine squares that all practice the skill, with a must-do square in the middle. The squares take about the same time and use different ways of working. Grouping plan Uses real names, or groups do not change. Groups come from the made-up results with codes, and the plan says when and how students move. Names the re-check, such as an exit ticket, that moves students. Fairness check The fairness checks were not run. All four checks (same goal, movement, patterns, access) were run and failures fixed. Can say what changed because of the check. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does the "same goal" fairness check ask?
options: Do all groups get the same worksheet?
Does every student practice the grade-level objective?
Do all groups finish at the same time?
Do all students get the same score?
check.why: Differentiation must not leave some students away from the grade-level goal.

check.q: Over the unit, the same students from one background are always in the support group. What would you do?
options: Keep them there, since it is working
Move them to extension without evidence
Stop using groups
Ask why, and check whether the grouping reflects the skill or something else
check.why: A pattern like this is a warning sign that differentiation is becoming lower expectations.
